title: US Judge Allows Meta to Proceed With Layoffs Despite AI Discrimination Claims From 26 Employees
excerpt: A federal judge in Oakland rejected a bid to block Meta's job cuts, ruling that the workers could not demonstrate irreparable harm, in what appears to be the first lawsuit challenging AI-driven layoffs at a major US company.
body:
• US District Judge William Orrick in Oakland refused to block Meta from laying off 26 employees who claim the company's AI tools targeted workers with disabilities or those on medical leave.
  • The lawsuit appears to be the first against a major US company to challenge AI-powered decision-making in conducting mass layoffs.
  • Meta notified nearly 8,000 employees — about 10 percent of its global workforce — of job cuts in May as it redirects resources toward artificial intelligence.
  • The workers allege Meta's internal AI systems tracked productivity, keystrokes, and AI token usage to rank employees for termination, disadvantaging those on protected leave.

A US federal judge on Friday declined to stop Meta Platforms from laying off 26 employees who filed a lawsuit claiming the company used artificial intelligence to target workers with disabilities and those on medical leave for job cuts.

US District Judge William Orrick in Oakland, California, ruled that the workers had not demonstrated the "irreparable harm" required for an emergency order blocking the layoffs, which are set to begin on July 22. The merits of their claims will be decided in private arbitration.

How AI Allegedly Drove the Cuts

The lawsuit, filed on July 13 in federal court in Oakland, accuses Meta of using what the plaintiffs describe as a "constellation of internal artificial-intelligence systems" to decide who should lose their jobs. Rather than relying on human judgment based on merit and work quality, Meta allegedly deployed AI tools to "score, rank, and select" employees for termination, according to the complaint.

"The workers allege Meta violated the Family and Medical Leave Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Pregnancy Discrimination Act, and the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act."

"The workers allege Meta violated the Family and Medical Leave Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Pregnancy Discrimination Act, and the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act."

Among the tools cited are a large language model assistant known as "Metamate," an employee-trained "second brain" that tracks communications and work output, and a productivity scoring system based on keystrokes, screen monitoring, emails, and internet search history. The plaintiffs — a group of anonymous managers, engineers, scientists, and researchers from California, New York, and Washington, DC — claim these tools failed to account for protected leave, effectively penalizing workers for exercising their legal rights.

"The legal question won't be whether an employer used AI but whether it blindly trusted it."

— Jon Hyman, Chair of Employment Practice, Wickens Herzer Panza

Meta has denied the allegations. "Workforce management and organizational decisions were and are made by people, not AI," a company spokesperson said.

A Precedent-Setting Case

The case appears to be the first against a major US company to challenge the use of AI in conducting layoffs. The workers allege Meta violated the Family and Medical Leave Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Pregnancy Discrimination Act, and the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act. They also claim the company failed to test its AI systems for bias, in violation of recently adopted laws in California and New York City.

A separate ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco recently found that enterprise software company Workday must face a class-action lawsuit alleging its AI screening software discriminates against job applicants, signaling growing judicial scrutiny of AI in employment decisions.

Impact on H-1B and Immigrant Workers

Meta's May layoffs affected nearly 8,000 employees, about 10 percent of its global workforce, as the company increased AI investments and reorganized internally. CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said he does not expect further company-wide layoffs this year, but another 7,000 staffers were reassigned to AI-focused roles.

For Indian H-1B visa holders at Meta and other tech companies, AI-driven layoffs carry an additional burden. Laid-off H-1B workers face a strict 60-day window to find new sponsorship, switch visa status, or leave the country. If AI tools disproportionately penalize workers who took medical or family leave — a group that may include visa holders managing cross-border family obligations — the consequences extend beyond job loss to potential deportation.

Meta has offered affected employees severance covering 16 weeks of base pay plus two additional weeks per year of service, alongside 18 months of healthcare coverage.

What's Next

The plaintiffs' claims will now proceed to individual arbitration as required by Meta's employment agreements. The court's refusal to issue emergency relief means the July 22 layoffs will go ahead as planned. Employment law experts say the case, regardless of its outcome in arbitration, will shape how companies disclose and audit AI tools used in workforce decisions.
